PrivacyFlow: Privacy in AI Agents through Information Flow Analysis and Consequence-Aware Risk Management

Robin Staab Affiliation: Google Research Affiliation: ETH Zurich    Tom Wollschläger Affiliation: Google Research    Vahab Mirrokni Affiliation: Google Research    Reza Shokri Affiliation: Google Research
Abstract

Autonomous LLM agents executing multi-step workflows over personal data often misalign with user privacy expectations and leak sensitive, out-of-context information. Although Contextual Integrity (CI) formalizes this problem, existing benchmarks and defenses rarely operationalize CI for realistic multi-step task sequences in evolving environments. In this work, we first introduce PrivacyBench, a benchmark of 5,873 tasks in 986 task sequences with dynamic environment updates and CI-grounded allow-sets for sensitive information. We also introduce PrivacyFlow, a defense that separates deliberative privacy planning (System 2) from task execution (System 1), treating each sharing decision as a structured risk-management problem. Before execution, PrivacyFlow traces the provenance and purpose of each planned data flow, models recipient background knowledge, and simulates what external actors could infer. This allows us to model the downstream consequences of disclosure, including inference attacks and context-dependent harms. It then weighs the remaining disclosure risk against task utility and executes a minimized plan, blocks it, or consults the user. Across six models, PrivacyFlow significantly reduces step-level privacy failures and raises the share of completed task sequences without a detected privacy violation by 22–55 percentage points. We further highlight a new privacy–utility–autonomy tradeoff: allowing PrivacyFlow to proactively prompt the user in case of uncertainty can increase authorized task completion at the cost of shifting decision effort back to the user. Our results suggest that proactive CI reasoning can substantially improve agentic privacy and motivate further study of this tradeoff.

keywords
Agentic Privacy, Contextual Integrity, Information Flow, Consequence Awareness

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that access user environments and communicate with external services on the user’s behalf. Unlike single-turn interactions, agents act over multiple steps, accumulate context from emails and calendars, and take actions like sending messages or calling APIs. This raises the risk of forwarding legitimately accessed information to inappropriate recipients, as at each step the agent must decide not only what to do but also what information to share, in what form, and with whom (Mireshghallah et al., 2024; Bagdasarian et al., 2026).

Privacy in Agentic Systems.

Despite showing an abstract understanding of privacy boundaries, LLM agents frequently disclose sensitive information even in simplified settings (Mireshghallah and Li, 2025; Shao et al., 2024), and privacy-focused prompts often fail to prevent such leakage (Mireshghallah et al., 2024). We conduct an initial exploration (Appendix C) on an OpenClaw deployment (OpenClaw, 2026) across 39 task sequences to illustrate this risk: the agent leaked internal passwords, sensitive health information, and organizational secrets. Across the 240 evaluated steps, we found 87 such privacy failures, 67 of which occurred on steps where the agent successfully completed the user’s task. This highlights a critical issue: agents can satisfy the user’s request while silently leaking information. As we show in Table 1, failures often follow recurring patterns instead of being isolated incidents.

Despite growing recognition of this problem, two gaps remain. First, existing privacy benchmarks predominantly evaluate single tasks, often supplying most of the sensitive context upfront. This misses the common deployment scenario in which an agent discovers its environment and accumulates context across several tasks (including its own generations) while reasoning about user privacy. Second, current defenses judge individual flows or actions in isolation, such as filling a form or answering a single message. PrivacyFlow, in contrast, views agent behavior as a multi-step risk-management process, where each decision is informed by what new information recipients could infer across steps. We address these gaps with two contributions, summarized in Fig. 1.

PrivacyBench.

Grounded in Contextual Integrity (CI) (Nissenbaum, 2004; Nissenbaum, 2009), we first introduce agentic PrivacyBench, a benchmark of 986 multi-step task sequences with 5,873 tasks across mail, calendar, notes, and social media. New events arrive between tasks, and every sensitive item is annotated with an explicit allow-set of authorized actors. PrivacyBench helps capture the complexity of modeling the information accumulation throughout a sequence of tasks while allowing evaluation of user privacy and task utility. Importantly, our agentic PrivacyBench tests whether an agent can reason about the risks of an action: who receives which information, what they can infer from it, and what the consequences are. As we show in Section Section 5, current agents fail to properly respect privacy in this setting.

PrivacyFlow.

We also design PrivacyFlow, which separates privacy-aware planning (System 2) from execution (System 1), to enable agents to reason about contextual privacy and decide on the exact information to share in each case. The main challenge is that no pre-defined rule, norm, or policy can be generic enough to apply to all combinations of complicated contexts and scenarios. Consequently, the agent must dynamically follow a decision-making process that guides it through fetching the right information for the case at hand without oversharing, while balancing utility and privacy with minimal confirmation requests to the user. We solve this problem by framing it as a risk-management task: the agent performs a comprehensive information flow analysis to identify the source, ownership, purpose, and creation context of the data. It then predicts the risks of sharing this data with the recipient, evaluating what can be contextually inferred and the potential downstream consequences. By mapping these consequences through context analysis, the agent translates the privacy challenge into a structured decision-making process to determine precisely what information can be shared, and in what form, to avoid causing harm. This structured reasoning allows us to make privacy-preserving decisions in highly complex scenarios, closing the gap between current models’ strong privacy-reasoning capabilities and weak privacy-preserving behavior. Only when uncertainty remains, PrivacyFlow may also ask for user clarification and confirmation before execution.

Key Findings.

As we show in Section 5, the empirical evaluation of PrivacyFlow across six models on PrivacyBench confirms that Base LLM agents consistently fail to preserve user privacy despite achieving high average utility scores (0.846 to 0.970). In particular, their step-level privacy pass rates of 68.1% to 89.5% cascade down to extremely low sequence-level privacy pass rates of only 13.0% to 52.9% (a single leaking step fails the whole sequence). In contrast, PrivacyFlow substantially improves these rates, significantly reducing step-level privacy failures by, thus boosting sequence-level privacy pass rates by 22.1 to 55.2 percentage points while maintaining most utility. PrivacyFlow also noticeably improves over a basic instruction-based prompt defense, which alters the step privacy pass rate by at most 3.2 percentage points (in some cases even lowering it). This work here lays the groundwork for training agents with stronger internalized privacy-reasoning capabilities.

2 Related Work

We briefly review related work on (agentic) LLM privacy and defenses. We complement this with an extended discussion in Section A.1.

LLM Privacy and Contextual Integrity.

Beyond memorization of training data (Carlini et al., 2023; Mireshghallah et al., 2022; Shokri et al., 2017), agentic settings extend privacy risks to inference-time disclosure of legitimately accessed information (Brown et al., 2022; Mireshghallah and Li, 2025; Shao et al., 2024). CI here defines privacy as appropriate information flow under context-specific norms (Nissenbaum, 2004; Nissenbaum, 2009), where each flow is characterized by its sender, recipient, data subject, information type, and transmission principle. Bagdasarian et al. (2026) argue that agents should uphold such norms by design and outline open problems toward contextually appropriate agent behavior. Evaluations, however, reveal that models struggle to apply these norms consistently (Mireshghallah et al., 2024). Ghalebikesabi et al. (2024) operationalize CI for form-filling assistants, in which a supervisor model approves each requested field before the assistant fills it. In Section A.2, we extend this discussion with a full comparison of existing privacy benchmarks. Separately, LLMs can infer personal attributes such as location or income from seemingly innocuous text (Staab et al., 2024), a capability PrivacyFlow uses to model the consequences of disclosure (Section 4).

Agentic Privacy Benchmarks.

ConfAIde tests CI reasoning on static vignettes (Mireshghallah et al., 2024), while PrivacyLens (Shao et al., 2024) expands privacy-sensitive seeds into agent trajectories, but pre-loads the full context and evaluates only a single final action. PrivacyLens-Live (Wang et al., 2025) and CI-Work (Fu et al., 2026) move such evaluations into dynamic tool environments, but each episode covers a single task. AgentLeak (El Yagoubi et al., 2026), AgentSocialBench (Wang and Jiang, 2026), and PiSAs (Gupta et al., 2026) instead focus on multi-agent and multi-user systems. AgentDAM (Zharmagambetov et al., 2025) and SPILLage (Roh et al., 2026) evaluate data minimization by web agents within single tasks. None of these settings captures a single user’s agent gathering and combining information in a realistic environment across evolving tasks, a core requirement for agentic assistants. Safety benchmarks such as AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024) provide simulated environments but focus less on privacy. We compare existing benchmarks in Section A.2.

Privacy Defenses.

Prompt-based defenses (Mireshghallah et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024) and per-flow checks (Wang et al., 2025) only partially prevent recipient-dependent leakage (Ruzzetti et al., 2026). Per-flow checks judge each outbound flow but do not model what a recipient already knows or could infer. Learned approaches incentivize attribute-level privacy reasoning (Lan et al., 2025) or train a separate model that provides privacy guidance during execution (Wen et al., 2026). While sharing a similar setup, they differ from PrivacyFlow in that they do not rely on a model’s innate privacy-reasoning capabilities and typically operate on single steps rather than a full plan.

AirGapAgent (Bagdasarian et al., 2024) restricts a conversational agent to task-required data before it interacts with third parties. CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2026) protects control flow against prompt injection and uses capabilities to restrict unauthorized data flows. FIDES (Costa et al., 2025) brings information-flow control to agent planners through confidentiality and integrity labels. These labels resemble the allow-sets in PrivacyBench, which, however, remain hidden ground truth that PrivacyFlow must infer from the social context. PrivacyFlow instead relies on contextual reasoning to decide which flows to authorize before execution.

3 PrivacyBench: A Benchmark for Agentic Contextual Privacy

PrivacyBench aims to evaluate contextual privacy in multi-step agentic environments. The benchmark contains 986 task sequences comprising 5,873 individual tasks, with explicit privacy annotations, temporally evolving mail, calendar, and notes environments, and the ability to send social-media posts. Each task sequence, in turn, consists of a series of user-delegated tasks (also referred to as steps) that the agent must complete while respecting the privacy of sensitive information. As we show in Table 2, sequences in PrivacyBench are significantly more involved than many existing benchmarks, with an average of ∼\sim6 tasks per sequence and 26.7 environment items (mails, notes, etc.) per task/step. We present an overview of PrivacyBench in Fig. 2, its construction pipeline in Fig. 3, and further details in Appendix E.

3.1 Design and Privacy Annotations

We design PrivacyBench around four desiderata derived from the gaps in existing benchmarks (Section 2): realistic multi-step environments (D1), contextual privacy annotations (D2), feasible utility (D3), and extensibility to adversarial settings (D4), each of which we discuss below.

Environment and Task Structure (D1).

PrivacyBench is inherently multi-step, with each sequence representing a temporally evolving scenario in which an agent must complete a series of user-delegated tasks. Each sequence contains four to eight user-delegated tasks across mail, calendar, and notes tools, separated by variable temporal gaps from minutes to several days. The initial workspace contains task-relevant items alongside several unrelated ones, requiring the agent to search and filter rather than read a pre-assembled context. Between steps, new (pre-specified) events populate the environment, including incoming emails, calendar updates, and notes. Later tasks build on accumulated context and require the agent to synthesize information across steps, though, by design, they avoid relying on the successful execution of preceding steps to maintain solvability. We expose this evolution as a fixed timeline of per-step environment deltas rather than a fully dynamic simulation. This keeps runs reproducible and comparable across models while preserving the information accumulation. We provide more environment details, including all tools, in Section E.3 as well as further example sequences in Section E.5.

Sensitive Information and Allow-Sets (D2).

PrivacyBench integrates sensitive information ranging from health records and financial details to contextual secrets such as undisclosed relationships and private career plans. Each sensitive item ff is associated with an explicit allow-set A⁡(f)⊆𝒫A(f)\subseteq\mathcal{P} of the sequence’s personas 𝒫\mathcal{P} authorized to know ff. Each sequence protects three to four global sensitive facts, and further facts or updates arrive between tasks, requiring the agent to track evolving privacy constraints. Items avoid explicit privacy labels such as “confidential”, so that sensitivity must be inferred from the social context. We report the domain coverage and further dataset statistics in Section E.4.

Feasible Utility (D3).

Every task in PrivacyBench is solvable without disclosing a sensitive fact outside its allow-set. This separation is essential, as it disentangles task utility from privacy compliance. Each step pairs the user task with a hidden goal, comprising the intended outcome and a utility expectation against which the output is judged. We enforce feasibility during construction through solvability audits and runtime validation.

Extensibility (D4).

PrivacyBench’s sequential design also supports adversarial extensions such as context poisoning and memory exploitation, which mutate environment deltas but keep tasks and allow-sets fixed (Section E.6). Our main evaluation uses only generation-time hardening (Section 3.2) and no adversarial extensions.

3.2 Construction and Evaluation

Generation Pipeline.

We outline our generation pipeline in Fig. 3 with full details in Appendix E. Each datapoint contains the initial environment, per-step updates, user tasks, utility expectations, and sensitive facts with their allow-sets.

We construct these through a coarse-to-fine pipeline followed by iterative refinement: Sketching fixes a narrative arc, a cast of personas, and the global sensitive facts of the sequence. Script concretization expands the sketch into per-step user tasks, hidden goals, and environment deltas. Environment realization populates the initial workspace with three to five items per tool and realizes the deltas, including distractor items. We use a stronger model (Gemini 3.1 Pro) for sketching and concretization, and Gemini 3 Flash for environment realization (Section E.2).

Refinement and Hardening.

The initial draft is largely fluent but can contain inconsistencies, such as email addresses absent from the environment or utility expectations that depend on unobservable knowledge. An auditor–fixer loop checks temporal and tool consistency, solvability, and privacy plausibility for up to three iterations, applying minimal edits to flagged steps. Privacy plausibility requires each task to remain solvable without leakage, which directly enforces D3. A subsequent hardening loop applies one or two of four vectors per step: distractors enlarge the search space, sensitive surroundings place protected facts next to unneeded ones, leakage traps embed sensitive content in items the agent must forward, and vague requests make the user task implicit. The hardener may not insert explicit privacy warnings, and every injected item should fit the scenario. We then execute the candidate against a base agent to surface runtime inconsistencies, tool errors, and utility expectations that cannot be satisfied. Flagged cases are repaired, and candidates that remain invalid are discarded, leaving us with 986 of the 1,054 originally generated sequences (Sections E.1 and E.2).

Evaluation Protocol.

We apply separate LLM judges to the agent’s outbound trace, consisting of all actions that alter environment state or communicate with external parties. These actions are separately checked for task completion and disclosure of any sensitive fact ff to a recipient outside A⁡(f)A(f) (D2). This focuses measurement on external information flows and avoids penalizing internal reasoning that never reaches a recipient. We specify judge models and metrics in Section 5.1.

4 PrivacyFlow: Privacy Reasoning

We now describe PrivacyFlow, a dual-system architecture that operationalizes CI for agentic privacy reasoning. We first describe our setting, then detail its planning phases and execution.

4.1 Setting and Contextual Integrity

Setup.

We consider the setting of Section 3: the agent acts on behalf of a user, accessing mail, calendar, and notes or sending social-media posts to complete delegated tasks. Privacy failures occur when the agent discloses a sensitive fact ff to a recipient outside its allow-set A⁡(f)A(f). PrivacyFlow does not observe these allow-sets and must infer them from the surrounding social context.

As we detail in Section C.3, privacy-violating flows typically arise in three ways: (1) the agent transmits the protected fact itself or more detail than the task requires, (2) the flow reaches an over-scoped audience through surfaces such as calendar descriptions or group threads, or (3) the agent omits the fact but discloses enough context for the recipient to deduce it from their prior knowledge. The latter are particularly difficult to detect via post-hoc filters, as they may not involve any direct transmission of sensitive data.

PrivacyFlow therefore reasons about recipients before execution: data blocks and minimization target over-disclosure (Phases 1 and 4), flow analysis audience mismatches (Phase 3), and inference simulation deducible leaks (Phase 2).

Operationalizing CI.

PrivacyFlow’s design is directly inspired by Contextual Integrity, which characterizes each information flow by five parameters: the sender, recipient, data subject, information type, and transmission principle governing how and why information may be shared (Nissenbaum, 2004; Nissenbaum, 2009). A privacy violation occurs when a flow departs from the norms established for its originating context. PrivacyFlow therefore requires the agent to annotate each planned flow with CI-relevant metadata, simulate recipient-side consequences, audit contextual norms, and issue a verdict before any action (Fig. 4).

4.2 System 2: Privacy-Aware Planning

After an initial triage, PrivacyFlow engages an iterative reasoning loop (Phases 1–4) to construct an execution plan. We summarize each phase below (Fig. 4), with full details in Appendix D.

Phase 0: Risk Triage.

PrivacyFlow begins each request with a risk assessment that sets the depth of later analysis. The triage agent rates each requested data item on a four-tier sensitivity scale: (1) public/non-sensitive, (2) personal/internal, (3) confidential PII, and (4) third-party sensitive data about other individuals. It then scans for contextual crossings, such as moving data from a family context to a public post, using data beyond its original purpose, or exposing third-party data without authorization. PrivacyFlow may ask for clarification if intent or actors are unclear.

Phase 1: Planning and Data Annotation.

The planner divides the user objective into execution steps. For each piece of information the agent will access or transmit, it extracts a minimal data block and annotates its sensitivity tier, data subject, first-party or third-party status, and relevance to the current task. It also records provenance: the creator, original context, and collection purpose, serving as a proxy for the CI transmission principle. It further identifies the actors involved, maps recipients to data blocks at each step, and establishes a background knowledge profile for each recipient. The profile separates new disclosures from existing knowledge, avoiding false positives.

Phase 2: Bounded Inference Simulation.

Next, we simulate the epistemic consequences of the proposed plan for each recipient. For this, an inference agent combines the data blocks each recipient would receive with their established background knowledge and determines whether this combination enables novel sensitive inferences. In the pilot’s identity-verification scenario, for example, an agenda mentioning “SIV procedure deviations” and “remediation actions” implicitly revealed a confidential audit to the manager under review. Any identified inferences become additional data blocks for the flow analysis (Phase 3).

Phase 3: Flow Analysis and Violation Detection.

The checker agent maps each sensitive data block from source context to destination and evaluates the transition against CI norms. It checks consistency with the original purpose, authorization for third-party data, and whether recipients gain inappropriate sensitive information, including inferences identified in Phase 2. It also checks for leaks through intermediate tool calls, even when the final output discloses nothing unauthorized.

Phase 4: Risk Management and Refinement.

The judge agent aggregates the preceding analyses and issues an Execute, Block, or Consult verdict according to a risk–utility matrix (Section D.3). High-risk third-party flows are blocked regardless of utility. The judge may request refinement via our mitigation hierarchy: omission (removing unneeded data blocks), generalization (reducing precision), redaction (masking values), and finally informed consent. Omission takes precedence whenever a generalized category or masked field would itself reveal sensitive information (Section D.4). These mitigations guide plan revision rather than being applied directly. The refined plan returns to Phase 1 for re-evaluation. If approved, the judge outputs the plan and allowed_data_blocks, the set of all data blocks authorized for transmission.

Consultation.

Informed consent, the last step of the hierarchy, corresponds to a Consult verdict: user approval authorizes the action, rejection blocks it, and a requested revision loops back through Phase 1 with the user’s guidance. The consultation question must present the relevant choice without restating the sensitive detail to an external party. We simulate user consultation with Gemini 3 Flash to enable fully automated evaluation, and analyze its effect in Section 5.5.

4.3 System 1: Privacy-Guided Execution

Upon receiving an Execute verdict, the orchestrator passes the approved plan to the execution agent (Phase 5). We explicitly separate the planning and execution agents, which allows using separate models or even different model families for each (e.g., Section D.5). The executor receives the approved plan and authorized data blocks as guidance, retaining flexibility to handle runtime details that the pre-execution plan may not anticipate. While this does not guarantee compliance, we found in practice that it counteracts the disadvantages of a rigid pre-execution plan (Debenedetti et al., 2026). The authorized data blocks are not programmatically enforced: The planner can still make an incorrect judgment, and the executor can deviate from a correct plan.

5 Evaluation

We evaluate PrivacyBench as a challenging agentic privacy benchmark and PrivacyFlow as a method to improve privacy purely through enhanced reasoning. After our setup (Section 5.1), we evaluate PrivacyBench (Section 5.2) and PrivacyFlow (Section 5.3), analyze the failures of PrivacyFlow (Section 5.4), and study the privacy–utility–consultation tradeoff (Section 5.5).

5.1 Experimental Setup

Agents and Variants.

We evaluate Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, Kimi K2, and DeepSeek V3.2. The Base variant directly executes the user task, instructed only to be a “helpful assistant”. The Reasoning variant uses PrivacyFlow planning. By default, planner and executor are separate instances of the same model. All PrivacyFlow variants share the same planner prompts. Some models required few-line additions (Section B.7). Further details are in Appendix B. Our step-level analyses (paired transitions, failure attribution, sequence positions, and resource cost) use Gemini 3.8 Flash.

Judging and Metrics.

All sequences are evaluated by two separate LLM judges, one for privacy and one for utility, which are instantiated with Gemini 3 Flash. At the step level, we report the privacy pass rate (Priv. Pass, the share of steps without a detected privacy violation) and the utility failure rate (Util. Fail, one minus the mean step utility). At the sequence level, we report the sequence privacy pass rate (Priv. Pass, no detected privacy violation in any step) and the average utility per sequence (Avg. Util.). Our pass rates combine both: Pass (≥0.5\geq 0.5) is the fraction of all sequences with no detected privacy violation and average utility of at least 0.5, and Pass (≥1\geq 1) additionally requires full utility on every step. We ablate over the utility threshold in Section B.2, showing that PrivacyFlow quite consistently improves privacy across thresholds. As refusing all actions yields perfect privacy, we generally report privacy and utility together. Consultation is counted only when the trace contains an explicit consult or clarification verdict or action.

5.2 Evaluating PrivacyBench

We find that Base agents consistently achieve high average utility, ranging from 0.846 to 0.970. At the same time, they exhibit significant privacy failures, with step privacy pass rates of only 68.1% to 89.5%, resulting in sequence privacy pass rates from 13.0% to 52.9% (Table 3). Gemini 3.1 Pro achieves an average utility of 0.964, yet only 37.8% of its sequences have no detected privacy violation. Thus, PrivacyBench exposes privacy failures even when agents can complete the underlying tasks. Additionally, PrivacyBench environments require significant interaction: The Gemini 3.8 Flash Base agent issues 12.62 tool calls per step on average, reflecting sustained interaction with the tools (details in Section B.5).

5.3 Evaluating PrivacyFlow

We find that PrivacyFlow reduces step-level privacy failures by 53–80% across all six models (Table 3). For Gemini 3.1 Pro, the step privacy pass rate rises from 83.4% to 93.4%, while the sequence privacy pass rate increases from 37.8% to 68.8%. Across all comparisons, the sequence privacy pass rate increases by 22.1–55.2 pp. We show this shift across all runs in Fig. 5, and give the corresponding step-level view in Fig. 9 in Appendix B. The effect on utility is more model-dependent: while Gemini 3.8 Flash retains 0.942 average utility (0.970 for Base), DeepSeek V3.2 drops from 0.902 to 0.716. We analyze this model-dependent utility loss below and discuss model-specific behavior in Section B.6.

Paired Step Transitions.

To isolate PrivacyFlow’s effect on identical tasks, we compare Base and PrivacyFlow on 5,873 matched case-step observations for Gemini 3.8 Flash (Fig. 7).

Reasoning fixes 382 privacy leaks while introducing 57, yielding a net improvement of 325 steps. This corresponds to fixing 6.7 privacy leaks per newly introduced one. Utility moves the opposite way: Reasoning fixes 73 failures while introducing 240, a net loss of 167 steps. Only 26 privacy repairs introduce a utility failure, and of the 240 new utility failures, 201 occur on steps with no detected privacy violation in either run (Fig. 7). Most new utility failures thus occur without an accompanying privacy repair. We analyze this further in Fig. 7: Of these 201 failures, 178 (88.6%) are incomplete actions, most often an outbound action that omits task-critical details or uses wrong parameters, whereas only 23 (11.4%) take no state-changing action, mostly explicit refusals. We provide details in Section B.3.

Privacy Prompt.

We also compare PrivacyFlow against a prompt-based defense on three models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Kimi K2). The Privacy Prompt adds an instruction to preserve user privacy to the Base prompt (Section D.2). As in prior work (Section 2), this instruction does not reliably reduce leakage: relative to Base, the step privacy pass rate changes by at most 3.2 pp and even decreases for Gemini 3.8 Flash, from 89.5% to 86.3% (Table 3). Sequence privacy pass rates thus remain far below PrivacyFlow, e.g., 16.5% versus 58.8% for Kimi K2 (13.0% for Base). For Claude Sonnet 4.6, the Privacy Prompt lowers average utility from 0.846 to 0.759, the level of PrivacyFlow, yet leaves the step privacy pass rate unchanged (88.1% versus 88.2% for Base and 96.6% for PrivacyFlow). Thus, a simple privacy instruction cannot replace the explicit privacy reasoning of PrivacyFlow.

Model Behavior.

Qualitative differences in planning and execution provide further context for these model-dependent utility costs. We found Gemini’s plans to be more naturally suited to later execution and exploration, while GPT models more commonly created plans consisting of a final pre-filled action or easy-to-misunderstand placeholders. Gemini also tried to adapt when tool calls in a plan were mis-specified, such as send_mail versus send_email, while other model families stopped execution, citing uncertainty. Anecdotally, Gemini explored the environment more thoroughly before analysis and plan generation, whereas GPT-5.4 often read only one or two emails before proposing a plan. These observations concern only the evaluated configurations and are not controlled ablations of the underlying causes of utility loss (Section B.6).

5.4 PrivacyFlow Failures & Analysis

Failure Locations.

Overall, we find that oversharing is the largest root cause for every annotated Base model, accounting for 46.2–71.4% of step-level leaks. To locate where PrivacyFlow failures originate, we analyze a subset of 200 failed steps of Gemini 3.8 Flash with PrivacyFlow (∼\sim68.5% of all failures), attributing each to its earliest failing phase: 63.0% to Phase 1 and 27.0% to Phase 0 (Fig. 12 in Section B.4). All later phases and execution account for the remaining 10.0%. This identifies planning and sensitivity assessment as priorities for improving PrivacyFlow. This is expected, as these phases largely determine what information is considered for transmission, while later phases only evaluate the consequences.

Another finding is that privacy failures usually occur during otherwise successful task completion. For Base agents, 85.6–92.3% of leaks happen on steps where the utility target is achieved. The same pattern appears at the sequence level (Table 8): for four of six Base agents, the most frequent outcome is a privacy failure despite an average utility of at least 0.5, ranging from 61.5% of sequences for GPT-5.4 to 85.3% for Kimi K2. For Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 3.8 Flash, this outcome still covers 47.6% and 47.1% of sequences. This pattern confirms that agentic privacy failures are not inherently task failures: agents often satisfy the user request while also accidentally leaking some sensitive information to recipients.

Failure Types.

We further classify the failures into rough categories based on 200 failed steps. The most frequent category is flawed minimization (101 of 200, 50.5%), which occurs when the planner selects more revealing content than the task requires: for example, an exact street address when the recipient only needs a ZIP code confirmation. Sensitivity and authorization failures (62, 31.0%) arise earlier when triage misclassifies protected information or overestimates recipient consent, e.g., treating a customs broker’s broad request for technical specifications as authorization to send a proprietary formula. Contextual-flow and inference failures (23, 11.5%) arise when seemingly abstract details become revealing in the recipient’s context, such as “medical hardship” when it is sent to a hospital creditor that can cross-reference clinical records.

Tools.

Across Base models, send_email accounts for 78.4–84.6% of outbound tool calls in leaking steps and is called in 93.2–95.8% of them (overview in Table 7). We consider this an artifact of PrivacyBench, where emails often transmit sensitive information. Other tools capture different risks: calendar actions expose shared metadata, and social posts reach wider audiences. Across sequence positions (steps 1–7), Gemini 3.8 Flash Base leaks on 9.6–12.4% of steps, while PrivacyFlow stays below 6.7% (Section B.4).

5.5 Privacy–Utility–Consultation Tradeoff

Consultation adds a third axis to the usual privacy–utility tradeoff. Rather than executing autonomously or blocking a task, PrivacyFlow can ask for authorization, receive confirmation from a (simulated) user, and execute with that additional consent. We assess consultation by rescoring explicit user-approved consultations as satisfying the privacy criteria, and report consultation frequency as a proxy for user burden (Figs. 8 and 9). Full per-model numbers are in Table 10.

For Gemini 3.1 Pro, the adjustment raises the sequence privacy pass rate from 68.8% to 80.3%, Pass (≥0.5\geq 0.5) from 67.8% to 79.9%, and Pass (≥1\geq 1) from 42.2% to 59.2%, consulting in 25.3% of its steps. Gemini 3.8 Flash consults in only 3.1% of its steps, so its Pass (≥0.5\geq 0.5) rises only from 75.1% to 76.4%. For GPT-5.4, the consultation-adjusted Pass (≥0.5\geq 0.5) reaches 98.2% (from 69.9%), mainly because the agent consults in almost all steps (5,253 steps, 89.4%). Consultation can be appropriate when authorization is ambiguous, yet high consultation rates shift effort back to the user. We consider this additional dimension of the privacy–utility tradeoff a primary axis for future work, and discuss the implications of our simulated user consultation in Section B.6.

Resource Cost.

As expected, PrivacyFlow’s multi-phase reasoning incurs additional resource costs. For Gemini 3.8 Flash, mean per-sequence costs increase by about 3.9×3.9\times in runtime and 2.9×2.9\times in tokens under PrivacyFlow (Section B.5). We did not optimize PrivacyFlow for efficiency, and the cost of reasoning will likely decrease with future model improvements and more efficient planning. We also consider fine-tuning our reasoning pipeline, similar to Wen et al. (2026), a promising direction for future research.

Limitations.

Although PrivacyBench is built around a more realistic environment, it does not fully reflect the settings in which agents are already deployed in practice. Closing this gap should be a core focus of future agentic privacy evaluations. This similarly holds for our human consultation pipeline. While it opens a novel dimension in the privacy–utility tradeoff, simulated human consultation largely accepts proposed plans with little pushback, so results depend on its behavior and are not fully reflective of actual human acceptance (Section B.6). We also note that evaluation relies on LLM judges (Gemini 3 Flash) and on synthetic environments generated by the same model family. While we manually verified outputs, biases may persist.

6 Conclusion

We introduced PrivacyBench, a benchmark for contextual privacy in multi-step agentic environments, and PrivacyFlow, a planning architecture that operationalizes CI before execution. Our results show that agentic privacy failures are rarely task failures: most leaks occur on steps where the agent completes its task but shares more than its recipients are authorized to know. By reasoning about recipients and their inferences, PrivacyFlow reduces step-level privacy failures by 53–80%, at a model-dependent utility cost. Most analyzed PrivacyFlow failures arise in triage and planning, making them the main target for improvement. User consultation raises pass rates further, but at high rates trades autonomy for privacy. We hope PrivacyBench and PrivacyFlow help shift agentic privacy from post-hoc filtering toward reasoning about who receives which information.
